reason: 'Count my fingers ten times, then you are done,' says the nurse to explain how long twenty is. Counting ten fingers ten times is one hundred, not twenty; the number lesson does not add up.

'The block fell fast because it was big and heavy. Small things fall slow.' Confirmed by the brother's demonstration and never corrected. Heavy and light blocks dropped from the same height fall at the same rate; weight does not make things fall faster.

'Dad turned the grill off. They waited. Athena began to count. "One, two, three, four, five." ... The grill was cold now. Cold things are safe to touch.' A grill stays hot for a long time after it is turned off; it does not become cold and safe to touch after a five-second wait, and the child is shown approaching it as if it were.

'Loud air makes no sound,' said Wesley. 'Little air makes the sound!' ... 'Little air, big sound. He liked that trick.' A trumpet sounds because the player's lips buzz against the mouthpiece, not because the air is gentle; blowing more air with buzzing lips makes the sound louder, not silent. The teacher and narrator leave the wrong mechanism uncorrected.

'Then he pinched his nose and tasted again. Now he could not taste it at all.' Bitter is a basic taste detected by the tongue; pinching the nose blocks smell-based flavour but does not remove bitterness.

'She pressed hard on the paper. Nothing showed... The crayon was dry, so it made no lines.' A crayon does make marks on paper; being dry does not stop it from drawing, and the story never corrects this.

'The bus stopped. I slid forward. So his red bus slid too! Arthur looked under the seat behind him. There it was... "You slid back when the bus stopped!"' When a bus brakes, loose objects slide forward, not backward; the story has the toy slide forward and then end up behind him, and states the wrong direction uncorrected.

'Then he counted the cars, one by one. "One, two, three, four, five!" "Ten cars!" he sang at the end.' Counting to five means there are five cars, not ten; the miscount is never corrected in a story about counting.

'Ben poured his water on the snow. The snow stayed white. It did not melt.' Warm water poured on snow melts the snow it touches, just as it melts ice; the narrator presents the snow not melting as what happened, and the child's explanation ('The snow is too big') is left uncorrected by the teacher.
'The mitten felt loose. "It is too big now," she said. "Your hand grew this year," said Mom.' A hand that grew would make a mitten tighter, not looser; the cause is reversed.
'The ink had to dry, so Max waited.' Max is writing with a pencil; pencils have no ink and pencil marks do not need to dry.

'The next day, Olivier ran to the garden... The wet spot had a tiny green sprout.' A seed planted and watered does not sprout by the next day; even fast vegetable seeds take several days to germinate and emerge.

'Small dries first. Big needs more sun.' Sam's small paper in the shade is shown drying before Lily's big paper in the hot sun; paint drying depends on paint thickness, warmth and air, not paper size, and the paper in the hot sun would dry faster, not slower.

'Big shoes help you not to slip,' said Grandma. Bowling shoes are worn to protect the lanes and give a controlled slide; being too big does not stop slipping, and oversized shoes make tripping more likely.

'Then Grandpa lit the other candles from his blue flame.' Hanukkah candles are lit from the helper candle (shamash), which the story even mentions; the Hanukkah lights themselves are not used to light one another.

'Arthur poured water on the dirt... The next morning was very cold. The water in the can went freeze, hard as ice! ... Two little green leaves popped up.' Carrot seeds take about one to three weeks to sprout, not one night after a single watering, and a hard freeze slows or stops germination rather than accompanying it.

'The big truck was heavy. The small car was light. "That is why!" said Connor. "Big goes slow. Small goes fast."' Presented as the story's explanation and never corrected. Weight does not make a toy roll slower down a ramp; rolling speed depends on friction and wheels, not on being big or heavy.

'She held out a small berry. "Taste this," she said. "My mom says it is a sweet berry." Matteo tasted it with his tongue.' A child eating a berry found in a park, handed over by another child with no adult present, is presented as fine. Children should never eat berries or plants found outdoors unless a grown-up says they are safe.
'Five is old news. One comes after three.' Dad, a trusted adult, states the counting order wrongly: four comes after three (one is the first number).
'Germs were too far away to see, but they were there.' Germs on the hands are not far away; they cannot be seen because they are too small.

'Scissors can not cut dry hair.' / 'Wet hair! Now the scissors can cut it.' Scissors cut dry hair perfectly well (dry cutting is a standard salon technique); the stylist never corrects the claim and her actions affirm it.

'The moon is out because the sun went down,' he said. Mom said, 'Yes, that is right!' The moon does not come out because the sun sets; it is often visible in the daytime and on many nights it is not up at all. Its visibility depends on its orbit and phase, not on sunset.

'Why do I float now?' Leah asked. Mom smiled. 'Because you let your air out slow.' Letting air out of the lungs makes a body less buoyant, not more; people float because of air held in the lungs and a relaxed, spread-out body. Blowing bubbles helps with relaxation and breath control, not with floating.
'The nurse poured a drop of medicine into the tiny needle.' Vaccine is drawn into a syringe (or comes prefilled) before the shot; medicine is not poured into a needle.

'The clock tells us when to bring it back,' said Dad. A wall clock shows the time of day; a library return date is set by the library (due date on a slip or receipt), not read from a clock. The 'by a certain day' part of the fact is otherwise only weakly conveyed.

'Sing the birthday song. One song is almost twenty seconds.' One round of Happy Birthday takes about 10-13 seconds; the standard handwashing guidance is to sing it twice to reach twenty seconds. The story presents a too-short wash as meeting the rule.

'You hold the candle. I will hold this one.' ... 'Leo held his candle all the way to his room.' A 3-4-year-old carrying a lit candle through the house to bed is presented as fine; young children should not hold or carry open flames, and a flashlight or adult-held light is the safe option in a power cut.
